name: Helvetia Blue
lede: Helvetia Blue is a strong, purplish blue recorded by Robert Ridgway in 1912, its name possibly recalling Helvetia, the female figure long used on Swiss coins and seals to personify Switzerland, though our sources never say so directly.

sections.title: A likely Swiss echo, left unconfirmed
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature places this hue on plate IX, hue 51, tone k, and the ISCC-NBS system later classified it as a strong purplish blue, about 5.0 units from that block's reference color [1]. Neither source explains the name, and no entry in our library glosses "Helvetia," so the Swiss association stays a plausible guess rather than a documented fact here [1]. In Munsell terms the chip reads 6.9PB 3.6/11.1, a fairly saturated, mid-dark blue [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[cerulean-blue]] and [[cyanine-blue]], at 4 and 4.2 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a close match to this blue in 30 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.13 percent, and in 19 by the stricter within-painting measure, which makes it rarer than 62 percent of the named colors we track [2]. Inside those paintings it most often sits as an accent, 68 percent of the 19 [2]. It peaks in paintings from the 1900s, at 3.4 times the expected rate[2].

The earliest match in our archive dates to 1543, in a painting attributed to Bronzino, with the latest from 1952, 18 dated paintings in all, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. That earliest match is 369 years before the name's earliest record in our sources, 1912 [1][2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
